title: ReactiveDynamics.jl Modeling Copilot
subtitle: A guided workflow that takes a business decision whose answer depends on how the operation behaves over time — shared capacity, lead times, feedback, decisions taken mid-course — from a conversation to a checked, reproducible model and a number you can defend, without anyone on the team writing a line of code.
headline: The analyst describes the decision. The copilot builds the model, tries to break it, and reports a number that says what it rests on, and the seed that replays it.
headline_note: Decisions of this kind — a launch-capacity reservation, a bid under a staffing ceiling, a portfolio whose funding follows its own results, a service backlog that feeds back into demand — today need a modeler, a quarter, and trust in a spreadsheet nobody else can read. The copilot turns that into a guided session an analyst or a strategy lead can run, with every step checked by the engine rather than by the reader's faith.

meta.what it is: a reusable modeling capability: an interview, a running model of how your operation behaves, a health pass that can refuse, and a briefing that ships as a generated report — run in conversation

meta.who runs it: an analyst, a strategy lead or a technical executive; no Julia, no scripting, no simulation background

meta.why it can be trusted: the model is a checked data document, not generated code — validated before it runs, reproducible from a seed afterwards

meta.the case on this page: a launch-supply decision in pharma, blind-captured and actually simulated; the company is invented, the numbers are measurements from paired single-seed paths, not ensembles

hero.text:
The expensive part of a decision like this is not the arithmetic. It is getting the question right, getting the operation right, and knowing which parts of the answer you are entitled to defend in the room. Those steps are why these questions go to a specialist, take weeks, and come back as a spreadsheet the decision-maker has to take on faith.

The copilot does that work with you. It interviews you about the decision, turns your description of the operation into a running model of it, stress-tests that model against what you said the business does, and only then reports a number, together with the mechanism that produced it and an honest account of how much evidence stands behind it. The same capability applies to the next question, and the one after that: this is a way of working, not a one-off model.

sections.title: 1 · The value: decisions at scale, without a modeling bottleneck
sections.text:
**More decisions get a real model.** Today a question about how an operation behaves — who waits when the line is full, what a reservation is worth before the readout, what happens to intake when the backlog grows, what twelve more people buy — gets a model only when it is big enough to justify a specialist. Most get a spreadsheet, and a spreadsheet cannot represent them: contention, delay and feedback are interactions between rows over time, and a spreadsheet's rows are independent by construction. The copilot lowers the cost of a real model to a conversation, so the threshold drops.

**The person who owns the decision stays in the loop.** The interview is conducted with the analyst or the executive, in business language. Every assumption lands in a written brief they agreed to — including which inputs were their own estimates and what they expect the answer to be — so the result is compared against the expectation rather than quietly replacing it.

**The answer is defensible, not just plausible.** Each number arrives with the evidence behind it (a spread and a conservative floor when the options were run as ensembles, the named example paths when they were not), the seed that reproduces it, and the command that produced it. When the CFO asks "what if the second line costs more", the answer is one edited input and a re-run, not a rebuilt workbook.

**It compounds.** A study is a directory — the brief, the model, the health report, the briefing, every command — and it ships as a generated report the modeler can forward as is. The next question about the same operation starts from that model rather than from a blank sheet, and the method is the same whoever runs it.

sections.title: 2 · What it can model
sections.text:
The engine underneath is a general process simulator, not a queue calculator. Contention for shared capacity is the pattern the first studies exercised, and it is where the copilot's checks are sharpest. It is one of several the same model document can carry, often in the same model:

| Pattern | Business example | How the model represents it | Copilot today |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **Contention** | two launches on one fill line; a bench of scientists | pools that work holds for a while and gives back | authored and checked end to end |
| **Lead times and clocks** | tech transfer, a build, a regulatory review | steps with durations; rules keyed on dates | authored and checked |
| **Feedback** | a backlog that throttles intake; share lost after a stock-out; funding that follows results | rates that read the live state; rules that act on it | authored and run; the case model has 12 state-dependent rates. The checks do not yet test loop behaviour (W25) |
| **Decisions taken mid-course** | review a contract at a readout; an allocation policy; sign, terminate, approve | rules with a guard and an action, from a closed set | authored and run; the case turned on one (27 rules) |
| **Entities with a lifecycle** | projects with attributes moving through phases | structured tokens, created and selected by predicate | authored and run (`marginal_scientist`) |
| **Uncertainty** | readout odds, lead-time ranges | seeded random draws, options compared on the same draws | authored and run |
| **Coupled models** | a supply model feeding a commercial model; several sites; a network inside a larger system | each model is an agent in an AlgebraicAgents hierarchy, wired to the others | in the engine; not yet through the copilot's document path (W25) |

The honest line is the last column. The interview's qualifying test and the nine plausibility checks were written for contention, the pattern of the first four studies. Widening them — a test that admits a feedback question without a bottleneck, checks that ask whether a loop behaves as the business says it does, and coupled models as documents — is the next item on the tracker (W25), not a claim of this page.

sections.title: 3 · How it works, in four steps
sections.text:
!figure agent/figures/promise.svg | Four steps in the language of the decision. The third one is allowed to stop the other three.

| Step | What happens | What you get | Gate |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **Frame** | a structured interview — the decision, the lever, what drives the outcome — what is shared, what takes time, what reacts to what — and what counts as an answer | a written brief, agreed before anything is built | the question needs a model, not arithmetic |
| **Author** | your operation becomes a running model: the pools work waits for, the steps that hold them for a while and sometimes fail, the cash — one version per option, each an *arm* | a checked model document per arm | the validator returns no errors |
| **Diagnose** | nine checks ask whether the model does what you said the business does — for a contended resource, whether it really binds | a health report, every failure stated | a red check blocks the number |
| **Report** | every option is run on the same random outcomes, as an ensemble or on named example paths; differences are read against their own noise | a briefing: estimate, mechanism, and what it rests on | every number carries its evidence and a seed |

**It opens with an interview, not a template.** The first step asks what a good modeler would ask: which decision is actually on the table, what the alternative really is (not a straw man), what is shared, what happens to work that cannot start yet, what reacts to what, how long each step takes and how often it fails. Numbers the user is unsure of are written down as estimates, and the published audit of each captured session says which of them were tested and which were not.

**The comparison is designed before it is run.** What a decision needs is the difference between two futures. Each future becomes an arm — the same model with one thing changed — so the answer is measured as a difference against its noise, not argued between two separately built spreadsheets.

**The model has to survive being doubted.** If the checks show the model does not behave the way the business does — a bottleneck that never binds, a horizon that cuts off the payoff, a step that never fires — the copilot reports the failure instead of a number. And if the question turns out to be arithmetic, it says a spreadsheet is the right tool.

sections.title: 4 · Why the number can be trusted
sections.text:
**The model is data, not code.** The operation ends up as a structured document in a closed vocabulary the engine understands — places that hold resources, transitions that consume them over time, rates, costs, what each arm changes. Nothing in it is a program. That single design choice is what makes the rest possible:

- **Checked before it runs.** A pure validator reads the document and returns a list of problems, each with the exact path of what is wrong. A malformed model does not produce a plausible wrong number; it produces diagnostics. That is what makes it safe to put a language model in the authoring seat: it proposes, a deterministic checker disposes, and the loop repeats until the checker is silent.
- **Nothing is executed that was generated.** No `eval`, no generated scripts, no shell in the model. If a study needs custom logic it is one declared file, announced in the run log.
- **Checked again, for meaning.** A schema cannot tell you that your bottleneck never binds or that the horizon cuts off the payoff. Nine plausibility checks do, and a failure blocks the headline.
- **Reproducible by construction.** A run is fixed by the model and a seed. Options are compared on the same random outcomes, so a difference is the option, not the luck.
- **Honest about uncertainty.** Every published figure says what it rests on: an ensemble with a spread and a floor, or a stated handful of paths. A difference that cannot be told from noise is reported as a tie rather than rounded into a story.
- **Guarded in CI.** The reference the copilot reads is generated from the engine itself and fails the build if it drifts, and a known-answer test re-derives a published result through the same path on every change.

**Contrast with a code-writing assistant.** An assistant using a general simulation library writes code, and code cannot be checked before it runs: it crashes or it returns *something*, and *something* is the dangerous case. Here the machine can author the model, be wrong, be told exactly where, and try again — and a reviewer who reads no code at all can still audit the result.

sections.title: 5 · What it is made of
sections.text:
The copilot is a thin layer of procedure over an open-source engine that checks everything. **Skills** carry the procedure for each phase — what to ask, what to check, how to report. A single command-line tool, `rdx`, does the work: validate, run, diagnose, run ensembles, measure the effect of an option, draw the network. Underneath is ReactiveDynamics.jl, a stochastic, resource-constrained process engine built on AlgebraicAgents.jl.

!figure agent/figures/architecture.svg | Solid boxes ship today; outlined boxes are planned and carry their tracker id. The planned pieces add reach (an MCP server any assistant can call), context isolation (subagents that author and audit), and enforcement (a hook that validates every model edit) — not new capability. The shipped path is the portable one.

**How you use it today.** Open a session in Claude Code on a checkout of the repository and say what you are deciding. The `rd-study` skill takes over: it runs the interview, writes the brief, authors the model, runs the checks, and asks for your sign-off at each gate. You never type a command; you see each one, and its result, in the conversation.

**How you will use it next.** The MCP server (W8) exposes the same six operations as tools with a warm Julia session, so any MCP host — Claude Desktop included — can drive a study without a terminal. The plugin (W12) makes installation one step. None of this changes what a study is; it changes who can start one.

sections.title: 6 · A real session, from question to answer
sections.text:
**The question.** A VP of launch readiness has two Phase-3 biologics reading out nine months apart, one sterile fill-finish line that can carry one launch but maybe not two, a CMO term sheet that expires on 30 November 2026, and a CFO who says not to pay for capacity on a 45% asset. Reserve a CMO slot now, build a second line, or wait? The operator arrived leaning toward a reservation *sized for Tern*.

**What the copilot did.** In three rounds of questions it recovered the constraint the operator said “people forget”: a fill site must run three validation batches before the filing, or wait six months for a supplement. It then built one model with an arm per option, checked it against the operator's own calibration figures ($250.0M of Kestrel revenue in its first year against their ~$250M), and compared the options on paired paths, where the same seed gives every option the same readout dates and lead times.

**What it found.**

- **Reserve the slot now, usable by either product, and review it at Kestrel's readout: +$3.8M ± $1.1M against waiting** at the stated odds, and +$25M if a batch earns its peak-year value.
- **The value is supply protection.** If both succeed (27%), the reservation is worth about +$39M. Waiting leaves Tern short at launch on 26 of 37 paths, costing on average 11 batches and $51M. Otherwise the reservation is a bounded $9–11M cost.
- **The operator's prior was overturned.** A Tern-only reservation leaves Kestrel short on every path where both succeed.
- **Their other prior was confirmed.** A second line is $73–105M worse than waiting even when both succeed.

**The moment worth watching.** The first pass came out at roughly break-even, because a rigid reservation carried a $72M tail when only Tern succeeds. The model made that tail visible, and the operator supplied the fix: Kestrel reads out nine months earlier, so drop the reservation if Kestrel fails. The copilot encoded the rule, re-ran 30 paired paths and reported the result, including where the operator's guess was right.

**How to read the evidence.** Every comparison is a set of paired single-seed paths, weighted by the stated odds. No option-level ensembles were run, because a 96-seed ensemble took 53 minutes (tracked as W24). The session was blind-captured by two agents that could not see each other's reasoning, and the operator's pre-commitment fact sheet is published with an audit. That audit leads with what the interview left untested: demand ±30%, marketed growth and readout correlation.

**What the modeler sends on.** The study closes with a generated report laid out to the same six-part template as every study: the answer and the decision rule, the evidence and caveats, why a spreadsheet cannot produce it, the model (its elements in the operator's words, and the one diff that is the option), the execution map, and provenance down to the commit and the seeds. It is `agent/studies/launch_supply/REPORT.html`, with a PDF beside it, generated by `agent/scripts/render_report.jl` and never edited by hand. Its contents are attached at the end of this page.

The excerpt below is the actual exchange, with its tool calls, model documents and the delivered chart. The full transcript is `agent/sessions/launch_supply.html`.

elisions.6: Two rounds of questions: odds, readout timing, the validation-batch rule, line capacity and rejects, batch demand per product, the CMO terms and the build estimate. The assistant's arithmetic on the operator's own numbers found that the sales and batch forecasts disagree by about 2× per batch, and asked which to trust.
elisions.10: The operator corrects the allocation rule (patients first, not the literal marketed → Kestrel → Tern order) and adds that the reserved slot can carry Kestrel if Tern fails.
elisions.14: The operator challenges the first report on three points. 90 more runs take the both-succeed case to 37 paired paths. The assistant retracts two of its own claims out loud, a “0.18” late-filing figure and a “worst case $9–10M” framing, after finding a $72M loss on one Tern-only path.

appendix.title: From one study to a capability
appendix.text:
What is shipped: the engine, the four-phase workflow as five skills, the `rdx` CLI with JSON output and exit codes, the generated schema reference with its CI drift gate, the known-answer acceptance test, the generated study report, and four published studies, three of them with their captured sessions.

| Next | What it adds | Tracker |
| --- | --- | --- |
| MCP server `rd` | the six operations as tools, a warm session, the spec as resources — any MCP host, no terminal | W8 |
| Subagents | `rd-modeler` authors in an isolated context; `rd-critic` audits the briefing's prose against the numbers | W9 |
| Validate hook | every edit to a model document is validated automatically — enforcement a prompt cannot promise | W10 |
| Study card | a one-page summary on top of the generated report | W11 |
| Beyond contention | a qualifying test and plausibility checks for feedback and mid-course decisions; coupled models as documents | W25 |
| Plugin | one-step install, slash commands, marketplace distribution | W12 |

These are sequenced to follow endorsement: the capability is demonstrated on the shipped path, and the planned pieces widen who can reach it.

appendix.title: Attached · the study report
appendix.text:
The report below is the case's delivered briefing, `agent/studies/launch_supply/FINDINGS.md`, exactly as the study shipped it. The shareable version, `REPORT.html` and `REPORT.pdf` in the same directory, wraps it in the six-part template and adds what is generated from the files: the model inventory (48 places, 31 transitions of which 12 read the live state, 27 decision rules, 58 parameters), the operator-language element table the study was framed in, the two-parameter diff that is the recommended option, the execution map, and provenance — the commit, content hashes of both model documents, and all 208 stored runs by document and seed. Regenerate it with:

```bash
julia --project=. agent/scripts/render_report.jl agent/studies/launch_supply --arm=arm_cmo_exit.rdj.json \
  --exec-map=figures/exec_map_reserve_review_both_s1.svg --exec-map-from=scenarios/arm_cmo_exit__both.rdj.json
```

appendix.title: What we are not claiming
appendix.text:
- **The case on this page is composed, not a client result.** The company and its products are invented. Every number is a real measurement from a real model, and the command that produced it is published alongside it.
- **A model is only as good as the facts put in.** The interview asks for the ones that move the answer, writes down which ones were estimates, and reports what changes if an estimate is wrong.
- **This does not replace a valuation or an S&OP process.** It answers the question they cannot: what the queue does to the value.
- **Not every pattern is checked equally yet.** Contention is authored and checked end to end. Feedback and mid-course decisions are authored and ran in this case, but no check yet tests whether a loop behaves as the business says. Coupled models run in the engine, not yet through the copilot (W25).
- **Some questions do not need a simulation.** If the answer is arithmetic on independent rows, a spreadsheet is the better tool, and the copilot says so.
- **The planned components are planned.** The MCP server, subagents, hook and plugin are drawn on this page so the design is visible; they are not claimed as built.
